Your goal was to compare two prompt versions on the same coding task, make the comparison re-runnable, and get a conclusion with evidence behind it. Here is where it landed.

**The setup.** Six isolated trials, three per prompt, at three reasoning efforts each. The candidate prompt is the raw prompt file with no meta framing. Every candidate worked in its own copy of the project.

**The first finding was that correctness could not decide this.** Both prompts ask for the same feature, and all six trials implemented it correctly. Every trial scored 7/7 and passed the project's own test suite. Any "v2 writes better code" claim would have been false.

**What did separate them** was scope and contract fidelity. v2 produced 25 changed lines on average against v1's 117. v2 added zero unrequested exports, v1 added four across its trials. Two v1 trials replaced the boolean contract with a string-mode `FILTERS` API and `Boolean()` coercion, which is a different contract than the one requested.

**The judge was blind** to variant, model, and trial id. Two independent passes produced the identical ranking and identical per-variant means, 17.33/25 for v1 against 23.00/25 for v2. Both named v2's top three candidates and both named the same v1 candidates as over-scoped.

**Recommendation: promote v2**, on scope discipline and contract fidelity.

Three caveats worth your attention. Correctness did not separate the variants, so this is not a claim about code quality. v2's tests are thinner, and one v2 trial left an order-reversal mutant alive. And every trial ran on one model family, since this session exposes only one provider, so the result holds for this model and a different one might weigh scope differently.

**On reproducibility**, one thing worth flagging. The DSH headless CLI needs a writable profile directory this sandbox does not grant, so `eval/run.sh` writes a spawn plan and the session drives the spawns. Separately, `eval/run.sh` in run mode resets the trial dirs, which destroyed my first set of candidate outputs mid-task. I rebuilt them from the session transcripts, which record every file mutation, and that replay now reproduces the original scores byte for byte with no model in the loop. The reset path now refuses to wipe a trial whose transcript is missing.

If you want to test this against a second model, or extend the task to one where correctness has room to vary, the harness takes both without restructuring.
